statement.title: Reserve Bank of Australia monetary policy statement, 03 November 2026
paragraphs: At its meeting today, the Board decided to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent.

Inflation remains elevated and recent data indicate that it is broadly based. The inflation outlook has also been revised materially higher in the updated staff forecasts. This partly reflects higher fuel and other commodity prices affected by the conflict in the Middle East. But domestic capacity pressures are also judged to have been a little tighter than earlier thought. AI-related investment is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, and inflation in many goods and services remains high. Liaison indicates that many firms are experiencing cost pressures and are either increasing the prices of their goods and services in response or looking to do so. Inflation is now forecast to remain elevated through much of 2027 and is not expected to reach the top of the 2–3 per cent target range until late 2027, around three quarters later than previously forecast. This presents upside risks to inflation expectations; some measures are assessed to have risen lately.

The increases in the cash rate target since the beginning of the year have tightened financial conditions. The economy is slowing, housing prices have fallen significantly and the unemployment rate has risen. The forecasts see growth in output slowing further over the coming year, which is expected to reduce capacity pressures and help return inflation to target. Higher interest rates and falls in housing prices and turnover are expected to weigh on growth in dwelling investment and household consumption. On the other hand, growth in overall business investment is forecast to be stronger in the near term, including data centre-related investment. Employment is expected to continue to grow, but the unemployment rate is projected to rise by more than expected in the August forecasts.

There continue to be heightened uncertainties about the outlook for domestic economic activity and inflation. The Middle East conflict remains unresolved, and there are scenarios where inflation is higher and activity lower than forecast. Global oil supply disruptions are maintaining upward pressure on global and domestic energy prices and inflation. A period of prolonged uncertainty may also cause growth to be lower overseas and in Australia. To date, however, growth in Australia’s major trading partners has been stronger than expected, as the boost from AI-related investment has outweighed the adverse effects of the Middle East conflict. In Australia, weak productivity growth continues to constrain potential growth and there are uncertainties about the extent and economic effects of the downturn in the housing market.

Since the previous meeting, the data have confirmed that underlying inflation remains broadly based. Capacity pressures appear a little tighter than previously estimated and there are indications that higher fuel prices are being passed through to prices of other goods and services. Inflation is now expected to remain above 3 per cent for the coming year and there is an increasing risk that higher inflation expectations will become embedded.

The Board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high. Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target.

The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target. Accordingly, the Board will be attentive to the data and the evolving assessment of the outlook and risks to guide its decisions. Monetary policy is well placed to respond to developments, and the Board is focused on its mandate to deliver price stability and full employment.

Today’s policy decision was by majority: six members voted to increase the cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.85 per cent; three members voted to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.60 per cent.

points: Members observed that financial conditions abroad had eased somewhat since the previous meeting, with lower policy rate expectations, significantly lower oil prices and higher equity prices in many countries.
Members agreed that financial conditions were probably somewhat restrictive, and broader indicators showed that monetary policy tightening was starting to be transmitted through various channels.
Members observed that capacity pressures remained elevated and inflation was still above target, while indicators of activity since March appeared to show the economy easing broadly as expected.
Members noted that information since the previous meeting supported the view that the economy was operating with excess demand and widespread inflationary pressures.
Members agreed that leaving the cash rate target unchanged would best balance the Board’s inflation and employment objectives, and that monetary policy needed to remain restrictive.
The Board decided unanimously to leave the cash rate target unchanged at 4.35 per cent.

AUD:speech:062aeb5694eb.title: Real Interest Rates – Restrictive Amid Cross-Currents
points: Head of Domestic Markets David Jacobs says monetary policy has tightened over the past year in response to persistent inflation, and financial conditions are now clearly restrictive.

methodology.title: Base rate
methodology.text: The last rate DECIDED on or before the as-of date, including a decision that has been announced but is not in force yet (shown as 'from <date>'). The Fed is the midpoint of the target range.

methodology.title: Implied policy rate
methodology.text: Market instruments give the overnight benchmark path; the benchmark-to-policy spread (median of the last 20 business days, excluding +-2 business days around rate changes and month-ends) is removed to get a policy-equivalent rate.

methodology.title: Methods
methodology.text: EXACT: 1M month-average futures chain. CURVE: OIS curve - for USD (fed funds), EUR (EUR STR), GBP (SONIA), JPY (TONA) and CHF (SARON) the daily Eurex Clearing settlement curves: the overnight rate is taken as constant between effective dates and fitted to the published discount factors (least squares, one rate per interval, a small smoothing term only where pillars cannot separate two intervals), then the overnight-to-policy spread is removed (EFFR vs the Fed midpoint, EUR STR vs the deposit rate, SONIA vs Bank Rate, the call rate vs the BoJ guideline, SARON vs the SNB rate); a meeting whose effective date is beyond the last pillar is n/a. Otherwise an OIS forward curve averaged between effective dates. UPPER BOUND: 3M contracts whose window spans several meetings. PROXY: government curves / bills, with a basis measured only from tenors observed before the first effective date - without one ('proxy without short end') no bp, step or probability is computed and only the raw level is shown.

methodology.title: Estimates (ESTIMATE)
methodology.text: Where no contract isolates a meeting (CAD beyond the 1M CORRA chain, NZD bank bills), every 1M / 3M futures contract of the exchange is fitted at once: the overnight rate is constant between effective dates, each contract's average over its window equals 100 minus its price (days already past use the realised fixings), and among the paths that fit, the one with the smallest step changes is chosen. The step of an estimated meeting is its level minus the level of the previous point; a meeting no contract reaches is n/a and its move is inside the next one. No probability is computed for an estimate. NZD: bank bills are a BKBM level; the BKBM-OCR spread is an estimate (median of 3M interbank minus OCR over months without an OCR change around them), not a daily observation. If the actual BKBM-OCR spread is wider than assumed, every NZD point is lower by about the same number of bp.

methodology.title: Step and probability
methodology.text: For EXACT and CURVE the implied step at the next meeting is split into whole 25 bp moves (n = floor(|step|/25)) and a fraction p of one more: P(n+1 moves) = p, P(n moves) = 1 - p, in the direction of the step.

methodology.title: Cumulative bp
methodology.text: Implied policy rate after the last meeting of the year minus the base rate, in bp. Positive = hawkish.

methodology.title: Repricing
methodology.text: Change of the implied level at a fixed horizon (last meeting of 2026 / 2027) over 5 business days (1w) and 21 business days (1m); independent of decisions taken in between. The change of the cumulative bp is a secondary field.

methodology.title: GAP
methodology.text: Market minus bank, in bp: the Fed's median dot vs the implied rate at the last meeting of each year. Only where both are on the same basis.

methodology.title: Surprises and reaction
methodology.text: Surprise vs consensus: decided rate minus consensus. Surprise vs market: decided step minus the step implied at T-1 (EXACT / CURVE / PROXY with a basis only). Reaction: change of the implied level between the close of T-1 and T at the next meeting and at the last meeting of the year.

methodology.title: Pairs
methodology.text: Base minus quote, metric by metric: the current rate differential (carry), the implied differential at year end (both legs policy-equivalent) and its repricing (both legs need a change of level). The flag is the weaker of the two legs.

latency.title: Time from decision to site
latency.text: First seen = the moment the collector stored the statement; official time = the decision time in the bank's zone (the BoJ announces at a variable time: its own RSS timestamp). Target: within 15 minutes. An external trigger starts the collector at the decision; before it existed the statements were found by the regular runs.

how_to_read: Position = (policy rate − the bank's inflation forecast) − (neutral rate − target): the real policy rate minus the bank's real neutral rate. Need = the bank's inflation forecast − target. The forecast is the bank's projection for the published period that contains today + 12 months; the cell shows its measure, its period and the rate path it assumes. Position and Need use the same forecast, so they are not two separate signals.
Same scale for both: within ±0.25 pp neutral / near target, up to 0.75 slightly, up to 1.5 plain, beyond that very / well. Core inflation and the output gap today are shown under Need for comparison.

Why gives three readings, not a forecast of the decision. Taylor rule: neutral + 1.5 × (inflation − target) + 0.5 × output gap − policy rate, in pp, once with core inflation today and once with the bank's forecast, each across the bank's neutral range. Positive: the rule points to a higher rate; negative: to a lower one. Opposite signs: mixed signals. Same sign and all four ends on the same side of zero: robust to the neutral range. Otherwise: sensitive to the neutral range.

Bank: the rate path the bank publishes (Fed dots, RBNZ OCR track) or the rate path its forecast assumes, and the vote at the last decision. Market: the move priced by each of the next two meetings (bp vs the current rate), its change over one week, and the market minus the bank's path at the same date. Market data older than 2 business days is marked stale.
